ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Baris has a few dominoes as shown in the picture. He wants to lay them in a line according to the rules of dominoes, that is that two dominoes can only be laid together if the neighbouring squares have the same number of dots in them. What is the biggest number of these dominoes that he can lay in a single line?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: From the image, it can be seen that there are a total of 7 dominoes, from left to right respectively 1-2, 1-3, 1-4, 2-3, 3-4, 2-6, 4-5. Then reason: Regard each domino as an edge connecting two numbers of pips, and the problem becomes finding a longest path of non-repeated edges in the graph. The degrees of the various numbers are: 1 connects 2, 3, 4, degree 3; 2 connects 1, 3, 6, degree 3; 3 connects 1, 2, 4, degree 3; 4 connects 1, 3, 5, degree 3; 5 only connects 4, degree 1; 6 only connects 2, degree 1. So there are a total of 6 odd-degree points. If all 7 dominoes are to be arranged in a line, it is equivalent to an Euler path using all edges, but an Euler path can only have 0 or 2 odd-degree points, so it is impossible. If 6 are used, it is equivalent to deleting 1 edge, which will only flip the parity of the two endpoints of that edge, so 4 odd-degree points will still remain, and it is also impossible to arrange them in a line. Therefore the maximum can only be 5. And 5 can indeed be done, for example according to the point-number order 6-2-1-4-3-2, corresponding to dominoes 2-6, 1-2, 1-4, 3-4, 2-3, which can be legally connected.
